title: The Professor Falsely Accused of Murdering Students
text:
On Thanksgiving Day in 2022, Rebecca Scofield and her family took a walk to the park. Scofield, an associate professor and chair of the University of Idaho’s history department, checked her work email. “I think you need to watch this,” a stranger had written. Scofield handed her phone to her husband, who clicked the attached link. He told her not to watch. She did anyway.

On Thanksgiving Day in 2022, Rebecca Scofield and her family took a walk to the park. Scofield, an associate professor and chair of the University of Idaho’s history department, checked her work email. “I think you need to watch this,” a stranger had written. Scofield handed her phone to her husband, who clicked the attached link. He told her not to watch. She did anyway.

On TikTok, someone named Ashley Guillard was claiming that Scofield was responsible for the unsolved murders of four college students, less than two weeks earlier, in Moscow, Idaho. Guillard, a self-described psychic, also alleged that Scofield, a scholar of sexuality and gender in the American West, may have been having an affair with one of the female victims. She displayed screenshots of Scofield’s work phone number, email, address, headshot, and biography. “As you can see from here, she may have identified with the LGBTQ community,” Guillard said.

Scofield felt an icy cold flowing through her veins. She had been in Oregon when the murders occurred; authorities would ultimately say she had nothing to do with them. But in late November, with a killer on the loose and no clear suspect, it was Scofield versus the firehose of the internet, where conspiracy theories filled the void and truth became secondary.

Scofield immediately called her dean and the police. This was the moment, she later said, where “everything veered to the left very hard and very quickly.” For the next three-plus years, as Guillard posted more than 100 accusatory videos, Scofield sought help from her university and recourse through the courts. She struggled with a profusion of physical and emotional conditions stemming from the stress.

This February, a jury awarded Scofield $10 million in punitive and compensatory damages. (Guillard is appealing.) But in some ways, the order comes too late.

“Since that Thanksgiving, I have not felt in control of my life,” Scofield says. She hopes speaking publicly — which she is doing for the first time — can help other faculty members who are harassed online and put colleges on notice to have policies for protecting them.

When the four Idaho students — Kaylee Goncalves, Madison Mogen, Ethan Chapin, and Xana Kernodle — were stabbed to death at a house off campus on November 13, 2022, the nation reeled. For more than a month, fear paralyzed the small city of Moscow as investigators searched for a suspect. Many students went home.

Internet sleuths filled the information vacuum with theories about the identity and motivation of the killer. One of them was Guillard, of Houston. As @ashleyisinthebookoflife on TikTok, Guillard drew on tarot readings and “psychic investigation” to accuse Scofield of having a romantic relationship with Goncalves and orchestrating the killings to avoid exposure.

In one video, Guillard spoke over a screenshot of the University of Idaho’s policy on relationships between employees and students, claiming Scofield was worried about getting caught in violation. In another, she acknowledged that people had been reporting the videos to Scofield: “You have to realize that I don’t just do this for clout or because I have an opinion. I have a gift. I have the ability to read into minds, read into past events, and into the future. So, know that I’m not worried about you reporting to the killer.”

The posts kept coming. In one, Guillard asked the “spirit” how many years Scofield would get in prison. After a cut, she came back to announce that Scofield would lose her job and then spend her life incarcerated: “She may even have some sort of same-sex marriage in prison.”

Later, in court, Guillard would say that she had been “intuitively led” to the Idaho history department and inquired into each person on its website to determine if they played a role in the murder. All but Scofield came up clean.

Scofield maintained that she did not know the victims and hadn’t been in Idaho when the murders were committed. In late December, six weeks after the killings, the Moscow Police Department issued a statement saying detectives did not think Scofield was involved. A few days later, police officers arrested a graduate student in criminology at nearby Washington State University named Bryan Kohberger. He was ultimately charged. Kohberger drove the same type of car that cameras had captured circling the house the morning of the murders, and his DNA was found on a knife sheath left at the crime scene.

But by that point, Guillard’s videos had already been viewed millions of times, and followers who believed the accusations were contacting and harassing Scofield.

In a way, Scofield was not surprised to become the target of an online mob. She just always thought an angry student or politician would be the instigator.

The professor had built her life’s work in LGBTQ studies, examining the gay rodeo and people on the fringes of cowboy culture: convicts, queer folks, charros. Her research embraced the kinds of interests that red-state lawmakers and conservative influencers increasingly derided.

Because it was her academic background and university affiliation that had drawn Guillard’s attention, Scofield asked her institution for legal help. But Idaho officials declined to provide it. Feeling she needed to act quickly, given the harassment and an upcoming major surgery, she hired her own lawyers.

“I think that if circumstances had been different, and that if I had felt like I had a little more time — we were just trying to get it stopped — I would have tried harder to frame myself [to the institution] as a representative of the university at large, and that I was being attacked,” Scofield said.

After an initial cease-and-desist order in November went unanswered, Guillard responded to a second attempt on TikTok, saying Scofield would have to go to court if she wanted the videos gone. And Guillard escalated her attacks, posting more than 20 TikToks on December 18 and 19 alone.

On December 21, a little over five weeks after the killings, Scofield sued for defamation and demanded a jury trial. The professor said she had “to try to make a public statement and defend my professional reputation, my personal reputation.”

But it was clear that her university, beyond responding to subpoenas, wouldn’t touch her case. A friend organized a GoFundMe, and Idaho’s faculty union, an affiliate of the American Federation of Teachers, asked for funding through its state and national organizations.

“It was so obvious that I had not been attacked in a private capacity, but that I was targeted because I was faculty,” Scofield said. “I think that there was a growing awareness over the years for union members nationally that this was not just a personal issue, but something that’s probably facing a lot of people in the academy now.” Around the country, state officials and conservative commentators were increasingly scrutinizing colleges’ support of LGBTQ people and how issues of gender and sexuality were discussed in class, including in Idaho.

Jodi Walker, a spokeswoman for the University of Idaho, told The Chronicle in an email that university leaders supported Scofield as best they could within the scope of their roles.

“The university does not legally represent employees who are enduring personal legal battles,” Walker wrote. “This case, while it certainly derived from a horrible incident in our community, was a defamation case concerning her reputation and outside the scope of university legal representation.”

Scofield described her dean, Sean Quinlan, and provost, Torrey Lawrence, as individually supportive. They took down her faculty profile. Scofield taught the rest of the fall 2022 semester on Zoom. Quinlan declined an interview but said he tried to support her “with the same empathy and care” he knew she would have given him were the roles reversed.

When Kohberger was arrested on December 30, 2022, Scofield assumed things would calm down, but they didn’t. Guillard continued to post TikToks accusing her of murder. She started speaking about Scofield on YouTube as well, detailing the “murder plot” in a 39-minute-long “synopsis” posted in February of 2023.

Chris Hanson, Scofield’s best friend, watched and downloaded the videos as they appeared and reported back to her. Today he has about 500 files in OneDrive, including hundreds of videos and screenshots of reactions.

“You don’t really know who’s believing it and who’s not, who’s following her account because they think this is true, or is it just curiosity, or is it just kind of watching the internet drama?” Hanson said. The numbers were daunting. “There were a lot of people who liked them. They clicked the heart on TikTok.”

Scofield was not just concerned about being called a murderer. She was concerned about what would happen when people Googled her. In a first-person narrative filed in court, Scofield detailed her worries that publishers would reject her work and LGBTQ communities would hesitate to participate in her research. “An unfortunate trope in my field is that of the lesbian professor grooming younger female students for sexual relationships,” she wrote.

She went on to say that some members of “anti-education groups” already opposed her employment at a public university: “Ms. Guillard’s homophobic rhetoric and highlighting of my research augments that opposition, and I worry her false statements may prompt someone to take violent action.” Despite having spent $466.29 on security cameras and door sensors in the first few months of the ordeal, Scofield wrote, she still struggled to feel safe.

Guillard’s motive has never been clear. But her allegations that Scofield was having a relationship with a female victim are particularly sensitive given the sociopolitical moment. Ari Ezra Waldman, a professor of law at the University of California at Irvine, said queer academics or academics who study queer issues are at an increased risk of harassment under a Trump administration that has targeted both the professoriate and LGBTQ people.

“An academic freedom that is specifically about the liberation of queer people becomes an easy target,” Waldman said, when “a queer professor or a professor working on queer issues is at the intersection of two lines of right-wing attack.”

At home, Scofield functioned in a state of hypervigilance, repeatedly checking locks and sitting in her young kids’ rooms while also trying to avoid frightening them. Her family withdrew from the broader community. For months, unable to get a therapy appointment, Scofield self-medicated with over-the-counter drugs to fall asleep. She saw doctors for severe headaches, nightmares, and nerve pain, and was eventually diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder.

Her body, Scofield said, “was just kind of strangling itself over time.”

Eventually, she was able to find a therapist. But it was hard to dedicate so much time and energy to taking care of herself when she had other responsibilities.

“I come from this rural background: You get back up, you dust yourself off, you’re alive, keep moving, push it down,” said Scofield, an Idaho native. “I think I’m only kind of coming to terms with the fact that this is a marathon, it’s not a sprint. I couldn’t just go to therapy for two months and be fixed.”

As Scofield’s life was falling apart, her lawyers sought to clear her name. Guillard represented herself and kept posting videos as the defamation case continued.

A judge was skeptical of Guillard’s clairvoyance and dismissed her counterclaims that Scofield and her lawyers had filed a frivolous lawsuit and committed defamation themselves. The university disclosed under subpoenas that it had no records of Scofield teaching or communicating with any of the students, nor of any investigations into her for misconduct.

In June of 2024, U.S. Magistrate Judge Raymond E. Patricco ruled that Guillard’s allegations against Scofield were defamatory. He wrote that Scofield had demonstrated the “absence of any genuine issue of material fact relating to the falsity of defendant’s statements about her,” and that Guillard had failed to show any support for her statements other than her spiritual senses.

Meanwhile, Kohberger’s case was also moving through the courts. He pleaded guilty in July of 2025. (Sentenced to four terms of life in prison, Kohberger is now trying to take back his guilty plea.)

This past February, a jury awarded Scofield the $10-million verdict, which Patricco ordered Guillard to pay. Guillard asked the court to set aside its judgment in favor of Scofield, which it denied. She has appealed to the Ninth Circuit and discussed the $10-million judgment at length on TikTok.

Reached by phone, Guillard called Scofield a liar and alleged juror bias.

Did she still believe, despite all the evidence to the contrary, that Scofield ordered the murders?

“I couldn’t objectively prove anything because I don’t have the evidence to prove it,” Guillard said. “But I still believe my readings. ... I’m not sure why my opinion on it mattered so much to her and everyone else, but I still believe my divination.”

Walker, the Idaho spokeswoman, praised the jury’s verdict. Still, she said, it doesn’t make up for the “mental pain and anguish” Scofield faced. What the professor experienced was “unconscionable,” Walker wrote. “Professor Scofield navigated this with dignity and grace.”

Scofield said it remains hard to feel that she’s not somehow responsible — like she did something wrong to call this into her life.

“I understand rationally that that’s not the case,” she said, “but there’s still this concern that, Well, if I hadn’t pursued my dream of being a professor and having a job in which my photo was on the internet, then my kids wouldn’t have been put at risk.”

The saga is one of the first things Scofield, who has been promoted to full professor, talks about in class. She tells students that if they have an issue with the course content or with her, she wants them to talk to her instead of posting online. “I’ve lived through this before,” she tells them. “I don’t really want to live through it ever again.”

The case has shattered the separation between her private and professional lives. People are curious. Scofield says she would be, too. Talk of the accusations and the case arises at conferences and workshops, and Scofield and her collaborators have to manage questions when her name appears on a book cover.

She would like to see colleges formalize policies that provide exceptions to rules around course delivery so professors facing security risks aren’t forced back into the classroom. And she hopes professors in similar situations understand that “general-counsel offices will not see you as the institution.”

“If universities want to continue to be places where people can learn without fear,” Scofield said, “then they need to commit to helping their faculty when they are attacked.”

In all, it took a year and a half for Scofield to prove she was innocent of claims that have, by all accounts, turned out to be baseless — and another two years to have a jury put a dollar amount to the harm.

Much time has passed since the University of Idaho acquired and tore down the house where the crime occurred, since national media outlets left Moscow, since the students who would have known the victims graduated. Yet people remain captivated by the murders. A documentary, out this month, is the No. 1 show on Netflix. An answer to the question “why?” is still elusive. And that’s a ripe environment for far-out theories to keep taking hold and wreaking their own havoc.
